messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Clean pass through the repo's own `slopwatch` gate. ~255 words.

---

**What you actually know at 3 a.m.**

Checkout is failing. That's the whole alert. CPU sits at 34%, every dashboard is green, and six half-awake engineers are on a call guessing.

Someone rolls back the last deploy. Someone else greps logs on one box out of forty and hopes it's a sick one. Twenty minutes in, a senior engineer remembers that the payments vendor changed a timeout last Thursday, checks it, and turns out to be right. Afterward we call that good debugging. It was a lucky memory.

Here's the gap. Monitoring told you something was wrong; it could not tell you what, because it only answers questions someone thought to ask months earlier, while writing the alert rule. Every new outage is new by definition. Your dashboards were built for the old ones.

Observability is the unglamorous work of making a running system answer questions nobody predicted. It isn't more dashboards. It's richer data underneath them: a request that carries its customer ID, its build SHA, its feature flags, and the duration of every downstream call it made, so that at 3 a.m. you can ask "do these failures share a deploy?" and get an answer in one query instead of a war room.

Teams that do this stop treating incidents as a test of who has been around longest. The knowledge moves out of a few people's heads and into the telemetry, where a second-week hire can query it.

That's the argument. The rest of this post is how to get there without buying six vendors and instrumenting everything twice.

---

One thing to flag: the 34% CPU, the forty boxes, and the Thursday timeout are invented detail — swap in a real incident of yours if you have one, since the specificity is doing most of the work here.
